findings.title: workload_samples selects samples by their end and roll_up assigns them by their middle, so per-minute roll-ups lose CPU
findings.evidence: raw.py:199 'WHERE ts > ? AND ts <= ?'; rollup.py:110 'bucket_start(sample.taken_at - sample.interval_s / 2, width_s)'. docs/17-build-prompt.md:269 tells phase 1 to build minute and history files 'on the existing rollup functions'. verify-6/v6_membership.out.txt: 'interval 1 s, phase 0.2 s: ... 1 per-minute window 3540 (-1.67%); 2 widened window 3600 (+0.00%); 3 whole hour 3600 (+0.00%)'; '5 s, phase 2 s: ... 3300 (-8.33%)'; '2 s, phase 0.5 s: ... 3480 (-3.33%)'; 'sample ending +0.2 s from midnight is in file 2026-11-21; ... roll_up's middle rule in 23:59 (of 2026-11-20)'. The lead's bucket_membership.py re-ran with identical output (upsert variant: '118.0 of 3600.0 (-96.72%)'). The baseline test uses whole seconds (tests/test_baseline.py:426 'DAY0 + second + 1').
findings.impact: The P1 gate 'CPU-hours from the hourly tier match the raw sum within 0.1%' (docs/15:13) fails with real fractional clocks. If the gate is tested with whole-second fixtures it passes, and production minute and hourly CPU then runs 1.7% to 8% low whenever the tick phase is under half an interval. Under the middle rule a 23:59 bucket also needs the next day's file.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/rollup.py:110 and raw.py:199: use one rule. A sample belongs to the bucket [start, start+width) that holds its end: bucket_start(taken_at), and the query becomes 'ts >= ? AND ts < ?'. This is the same half-open split utc_day uses, so no bucket straddles two day files. docs/17-build-prompt.md Store: state the rule. Add a test that sends fractional timestamps through workload_samples and then roll_up.
findings.cost: About 4 lines in two files, one doc sentence, one test.
findings.verification: I re-ran the lead's probe and got identical output. I also wrote v6_membership.py independently. The loss appears only when the minute window is queried and rolled up on its own. A window widened by one interval, or one roll_up over the whole span, is exact, so the defect is a trap in composing the two functions rather than an impossibility. The brief directs builders into it (docs/17:269). R24 covers sums and covered seconds, and R13 covers the hourly source. Neither sets a membership rule. I changed the fix: the lead's '(start, start+width]' conflicts with utc_day's [00:00, 24:00) file split, because a sample ending exactly at 00:00:00.0 lands in the next file. I checked and dropped a possible edge effect: under steady load the end and middle sums agree (3600 each). Severity stays high because the gate fails, or the number is wrong, under real clocks.

findings.title: Nothing records which raw days have been rolled up and no order of catch-up and retention is stated, so raw days can be deleted before roll-up; retention stops while the server is down
findings.evidence: files.py:121-131: expired_raw tests file age only. verify-6/v6_tiers.out.txt: 'expired_raw(self, now: 'float', retention_s: 'float') -> 'list[Path]''. The lead's retention_calendar.py re-ran identically: 'server back at 09:00 on the 15th after five days away: expired_raw offers ['2026-11-10.db', '2026-11-11.db', '2026-11-12.db'] for deletion. FileMap members that record what has been rolled up: none'. docs/17:52: the collector 'writes the raw files and nothing else'. docs/17:53: the server does 'rollups, retention'. Grepping docs for catch-up, rolled-up and watermark finds no rule.
findings.impact: Suppose the server is down longer than retention.raw (48 h) while the collector keeps writing. A retention pass that runs before catch-up then deletes days whose minute and hourly buckets were never built, and that trend history is lost for good. While the server is down, raw files also grow with no budget enforced, roughly 0.4 to 0.7 GB a day.
findings.proposed_change: docs/06-storage.md and docs/17-build-prompt.md Store: 'The server keeps a rolled-up-until mark in the history file. At start it rolls up every raw day it holds, oldest first, before any retention pass, and deletes a raw file only after the mark has passed that day's end.' src/submeter/store/files.py expired_raw: take the mark as an argument and never return a day after it.
findings.cost: Two sentences in each doc and about 5 lines in files.py.
findings.decision_question: Who deletes raw files? Options: (a) only the server, gated on the rolled-up-until mark; (b) the server as in (a), plus a collector-side safety cap (for example, delete raw files older than 7 days, with a logged finding) so that a dead server cannot fill the disk. Recommendation: (b).
findings.verification: I re-ran retention_calendar.py and got identical output, and printed expired_raw's signature, which has no roll-up input. I searched docs/ and found no catch-up or ordering rule. R13 ('while those still exist'), R23 and R26 do not cover ordering. I downgraded from high to medium: the loss needs both more than 48 h of server downtime with the collector running and an implementation that runs retention before catch-up. Normal running loses nothing.

findings.title: synchronous=NORMAL does not deliver 'a crash or power loss may lose up to 5 seconds', and the kill test cannot detect the gap
findings.evidence: raw.py:70 'PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL'; docs/17:138 'Durability: synchronous=NORMAL. A crash or power loss may lose up to 5 seconds of samples'. Re-fetched https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html: 'A transaction committed in WAL mode with synchronous=NORMAL might roll back following a power loss or system crash. Transactions are durable across application crashes regardless of the synchronous setting or journal mode.' and 'In WAL mode when synchronous is NORMAL (1), the WAL file is synchronized before each checkpoint ... but no sync operations occur during most transactions.' Lead's wal_readers.out.txt: 'the log reached 3.9 MiB and was reset after 149 ticks. At a 1 s interval that is one log sync every 2.5 minutes'. The docs/15:13 gate tests only 'Killing the collector'.
findings.impact: On a power loss or OS crash, SQLite guarantees only the samples up to the last checkpoint: minutes, not 5 s, and longer at the idle cadence. The gate passes by construction, because a killed process loses nothing at any setting. There is no corruption risk.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:138 and R36: pick one option. (a) Run a PASSIVE checkpoint every 5 s, which syncs the log. (b) Use synchronous=FULL for raw files. (c) Restate the promise: 'a program crash loses nothing committed; a power loss or OS crash may lose the samples since the last checkpoint, up to a few minutes'. Either way, state that the P1 gate does not test power loss.
findings.cost: One sentence, plus one timer line in the collector loop if (a).
findings.decision_question: Should power-loss loss be bounded at 5 s, by (a) a PASSIVE checkpoint every 5 s (about 0.4 syncs a second) or (b) synchronous=FULL (about 1 sync per tick), or should the promise be relaxed (c) to 'since the last checkpoint'? Recommendation: (c). A few minutes lost at a power cut is a short gap that covered seconds already handle. Choose (a), measured in P1, only if the 5 s bound matters to you.
findings.verification: I re-fetched pragma.html; both quotes are present and mean what the lead says. I read raw.py:68-71. I did not re-run the strace part of wal_readers.py, which is heavy I/O while other verifiers are running; the vendor text and the code are enough. R36 states the promise but not the mechanism. I kept medium: the brief's promise is misleading, but only a few minutes at a power loss are affected.

findings.title: A quiet process's CPU is held in memory until a keyframe: a crash loses up to 10 minutes of it, and in normal running it is stamped up to 10 minutes late
findings.evidence: raw.py:138 writes a row only if 'full or moved or pending >= self._cpu_share * waited'. A process holding steady below 0.5% of a core never meets that. config.py:64-66 allows a keyframe interval of 1m to 1h. verify-6/v6_held_cpu.out.txt: '40 processes at 0.4% of a core for 900 s from 10:55: workload_raw holds 144.00 CPU-s, process_raw holds 96.16; a crash now loses 47.84 CPU-s'; 'process rows were written: [1, 601]'; '10:00 hour: these processes used 48.00 CPU-s; process rows stamped in that hour hold 0.16'. The lead's raw_store_cases.py re-ran identically: 'process_raw holds 1.2 in 300 rows; workload_raw holds 648.0'.
findings.impact: This contradicts raw.py:5 and docs/14 ('per-process sums stay exact') and the 5 s promise in docs/17:138. After any collector crash, process-level views undercount quiet processes by up to one keyframe interval. In normal running, every hour, quiet processes' CPU lands in the wrong hour of the hourly top-ten executables (R28). Workload totals are unaffected.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/raw.py:138: also write the row when waited >= 60 s and when the batch crosses a UTC hour boundary. docs/14-baseline-modules.md store.raw: 'a crash loses at most 60 s of a quiet process's CPU from process rows; workload rows lose nothing committed'.
findings.cost: About 4 lines and one test. The lead estimates about 10% more process rows.
findings.verification: I re-ran raw_store_cases.py and got identical output. I wrote v6_held_cpu.py, which writes through RawStore and reads with a second read-only connection standing in for a crash; it confirmed both the loss and the hour shift. The flush in close() (raw.py:227-232) runs only on a clean close. R31's keyframes bound how far back a reader must look, not what a crash loses, and R36 promises 5 s. I did not re-run the 12-kill crash_kill.py loop; my probe reproduces the mechanism.

findings.title: The write-ahead log is not truncated at each checkpoint as docs/17 says, and a long-lived reader grows it without bound
findings.evidence: raw.py:71 journal_size_limit=67108864; truncation happens only in close() (raw.py:233); docs/17:138 says 'truncate it at each checkpoint'. Re-fetched https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html: 'in WAL mode, the write-ahead log file is not truncated following a checkpoint. Instead, SQLite reuses the existing file'; journal_size_limit truncates 'to the limit'. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html: 'if there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.' Lead's wal_readers.out.txt: '110.1 MiB after an unfinished cursor was held across 4000 ticks (27 KiB a tick); 64.0 MiB 1500 ticks after the cursor closed'. files.py:152 counts history.db only, not its -wal.
findings.impact: Normal running leaves about 4 MiB of log per open file, which is harmless. After a long reader, such as a database browser the user left open on today's file, the log stays at up to 64 MiB per open file, and disk_use misses the history file's log. The baseline's reader uses fetchall (raw.py:196-201), and docs/17:138 already requires short reads.
findings.proposed_change: docs/17-build-prompt.md:138: replace 'truncate it at each checkpoint' with 'journal_size_limit bounds the log left after a checkpoint; store status and doctor report each -wal size and raise a finding when it exceeds that'. raw.py:71: set the limit to 4 MiB. files.py:152: count history.db*. Correction to the lead's fix: a timed TRUNCATE checkpoint cannot complete while a reader holds an old snapshot, so it does not bound growth under a long reader.
findings.cost: One doc sentence and two one-line code changes.
findings.verification: I re-fetched wal.html and pragma.html; the quotes are present. I did not re-run wal_readers.py (4000+ ticks of I/O plus strace while other verifiers are running). I downgraded from medium to low: the brief already requires short reads and the baseline reader complies, so what remains is a doc/code mismatch and up to 64 MiB per file after an incident. I also corrected the proposed fix.

findings.title: Retention deletes only the .db, so -wal and -shm side files are left behind and counted forever; an open reader defeats 'frees its space at once' on both systems
findings.evidence: files.py:124 globs '*.db', while disk_use (files.py:154) counts '*.db*'. verify-6/v6_read_path.out.txt: 'expired_raw returns ['2026-11-10.db']; deleting those leaves ['2026-11-10.db-shm', '2026-11-10.db-wal'], which disk_use counts under raw: 1081344 B after the .db is gone'. The lead's side_files.py re-ran identically: a mode=ro read leaves '-shm 32768 B, -wal 0 B'; a killed writer leaves '-wal 3926392 B'. Re-fetched os_win.c winOpen: 'dwShareMode = FILE_SHARE_READ | FILE_SHARE_WRITE;' with no FILE_SHARE_DELETE. DeleteFileW: 'The DeleteFile function fails if an application attempts to delete a file that has other handles open for normal I/O or as a memory-mapped file (FILE_SHARE_DELETE must have been specified when other handles were opened).' Python os.remove: 'On Windows, attempting to remove a file that is in use causes an exception to be raised; on Unix, the directory entry is removed but the storage allocated to the file is not made available until the original file is no longer in use.'
findings.impact: Orphaned side files, from a few KiB to a few MiB per day (more after a crash), are never deleted and count against the budget. The P1 gate wording 'Deleting a day of raw data frees its space at once' (docs/15:13) is false on both systems while any reader holds the file.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/files.py expired_raw and expired_minute: return each file's .db together with its -wal and -shm. docs/17-build-prompt.md Store: 'retention deletes the .db with its -wal and -shm, treats a refused delete as retry-next-pass, and counts space as freed only when the files are gone'. docs/15:13: 'frees its space once no reader holds it'.
findings.cost: About 6 lines and two doc clauses.
findings.verification: I re-fetched all three vendor sources; the quotes are present. I re-ran side_files.py and wrote v6_read_path.py part 4. Part of the lead is already handled: docs/17:112 ('Open closed files only for the length of a query, so they can be deleted on Windows') and docs/reference/windows-priorities.md:60 ('retention needs to retry later, which the build must plan for') already cover the Windows blocking and the retry. expired_raw is recomputed from disk on every pass, so a refused delete retries without extra code. What is new is the side files and the gate wording, so I downgraded from medium to low. The Windows behaviour itself was not observed here.

findings.title: The baseline's only raw-file reader is the writer class: reading creates files, takes the write lock and checkpoints the collector's log
findings.evidence: raw.py:66-76: RawFile.__init__ runs mkdir, opens read-write, sets the journal mode, runs CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and does INSERT OR IGNORE into meta. raw.py:233: close() runs wal_checkpoint(TRUNCATE). workload_samples exists only on RawFile (raw.py:195). verify-6/v6_read_path.out.txt: '1. reading a day with no file returned 0 rows and left: 2026-01-01.db 40960 B'; '2. RawFile opened while the collector holds the write lock: refused: database is locked'; '3. ... 2026-11-19.db 4096 B, ... -wal 1075352 B / RawFile read 120 rows and on close the .db went from 4096 B to 49152 B'. AGENTS.md: 'Each data file has one writer: the collector writes raw files'. Re-fetched https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html: 'If a database file is separated from its WAL file, then transactions that were previously committed to the database might be lost'.
findings.impact: A server that reads through RawFile becomes a second writer of the collector's files, which breaks the one-writer rule. It also creates files for days the collector never wrote, competes for the collector's write lock (with a 5 s busy wait), and checkpoints crashed files. Separately, a quarantine that moves only the .db (docs/17:139) loses a crashed day whose data is still in its -wal.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/raw.py: add a read-only opener (sqlite3.connect('file:PATH?mode=ro', uri=True), never immutable=1) that raises if the file is missing, and move workload_samples onto it. docs/17-build-prompt.md:139: 'quarantine moves the .db with its -wal and -shm'.
findings.cost: About 20 lines in raw.py, a test, and one doc clause.
findings.verification: I wrote v6_read_path.py and confirmed all three writes. I re-ran side_files.py: immutable=1 fails on a crashed file and mode=ro reads all 120 ticks. docs/17:112 says 'Open closed files only for the length of a query' but never says read-only. The cluster's second problem, quarantine moving only the .db, is kept as a doc clause. Severity stays medium: one writer per file is a design rule from AGENTS.md, not one of the three fixed rules.

findings.title: The 0.1 GB minute-tier estimate assumes an unstated compact bucket encoding and only 9 series, and the deletion order cannot keep the promised 'exactly enforced' 2 GB cap
findings.evidence: histogram.py:26-30,53-54: two scales of 64 bins plus 2, so 132 values a bucket. docs/06:111: '9 series, 1,440 buckets a day, 250 bytes each'. The lead's row_sizes.py re-ran identically: 'dense 8-byte floats, rowid table 1403 B a bucket; 9 series: 0.55 to 0.67 GB for 30 to 37 days; 26 series: 1.94 GB; 200 series: 14.95 GB'; 'filled bins only, plus 18 catalogue fields 311 B a bucket; ... 200 series: 3.31 GB'. The same probe measures raw rows at 48 B against the brief's 90 B. docs/04:22 'a 2 GB cap that is enforced exactly'. docs/17:141 and docs/06:117 delete raw down to a 24 h floor, then backups, then 'raise a finding'; minute files are never deleted. docs/08:32,34,38,54 promise 'raw retention about 13 h', below the 24 h floor.
findings.impact: A dense encoding makes the minute tier 5 to 6 times its estimate. With more series (doctor warns only at 200), minute files alone can exceed the budget, and the deletion order cannot reduce them, so 'enforced exactly' is false. The docs/08 status lines promise raw retention below the floor.
findings.proposed_change: docs/06-storage.md 'Disk use after a year': state the bucket encoding (sparse filled bins, about 300 B a bucket) and give the minute size per series, at 50 series and at 200. docs/04-features.md:22: drop 'enforced exactly', or add minute files to the deletion order (decision). docs/08-configuration.md:32,34,38: replace 'about N hours' with 'raw drops toward its 24 h floor; below that a finding is raised'.
findings.cost: About 10 changed lines across three docs.
findings.decision_question: When raw is at its 24 h floor, backups are down to one and the store is still over budget, should the oldest minute files be deleted (down to, say, 7 days), or is the budget a warning only? Recommendation: delete minute files oldest first down to 7 days, then raise a finding; never delete history.
findings.verification: I re-ran row_sizes.py and budget_arithmetic.py and got identical output, and recomputed the histogram size from the code. I rejected two sub-points. (1) That 72 h of raw plus 0.55 GB of other files puts the 500 ms row over budget: docs/06:110 already gives '2 to 3 daily files, 0.7 to 1.1 GB', and the lead's own measurement is 48 B a raw row rather than 90 B, so docs/08 overstates raw and its status lines are not shown wrong. (2) Binary versus decimal GB: parse_size('2GB') is 2.147e9 B, larger than the decimal figures, so no status changes. At the default 9 series even a dense encoding totals about 1.7 GB with measured raw sizes, so the risk is many series, not the defaults.

findings.title: The raw schema lacks columns for several catalogue metrics and never reads back its schema version, so the first schema change breaks the day's open file
findings.evidence: raw.py:41-52: workload_raw has one memory_bytes; process_raw has no I/O or handle columns; there is no per-core table. docs/06:82-83,86,90,120 promise two memory metrics with the age of the reading, per-process I/O and handles, and per-core load. SampleBatch (models.py:122-131) has no memory_total_bytes, although docs/17:121 says buckets record memory capacity. raw.py:72-76 uses CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS plus 'INSERT OR IGNORE INTO meta ... schema_version'. A grep shows SCHEMA_VERSION is only ever written (raw.py:31,75). The lead's schema_gaps.py re-ran identically: 'a version 2 collector reopened the version 1 file without an error. The file still says schema_version 1 ... Its 11-value insert then fails'.
findings.impact: Each missing metric forces a schema change. The first change that ships during a day makes every collector write fail until UTC midnight. Minute files live 30 to 37 days, so two changes in that window break docs/17:140's rule that 'readers accept the current and previous versions'.
findings.proposed_change: Plan, as a P1 task: put every catalogue column into schema version 1 of the raw, minute and history tables, nullable, with NULL meaning unavailable. Now: in src/submeter/store/raw.py, read schema_version on open; if it differs, start a new file for the rest of the day under a name that files.py parses, and teach expired_raw that name (files.py:126-128 skips any non-ISO name today). docs/17:140: 'readers accept every version still on disk'.
findings.cost: About 10 lines and two doc sentences now; the schema columns are a P1 task.
findings.verification: I re-ran schema_gaps.py and got identical output, read raw.py and models.py, and grepped for schema_version. The lead's third point, that rules.py:208-209 sums unreadable I/O as 0, is a distinct problem already carried by E-baseline#3 and F-consistency#13 in other clusters, so I left it out of this finding and its severity. Medium: nothing fails until the first schema change, but every missing column guarantees one.

findings.title: What starts an epoch is stated five ways and never settles adaptive cadence; a bucket spanning an epoch or core-count change keeps only the latest values
findings.evidence: docs/04:24 'Every change of settings, rules or hardware'; docs/08:5 'every change'; docs/08:116 'Any change to sampling, rules or providers'; docs/06:98 and docs/17:130 'the sampling intervals, the rules file, each provider's status, the hardware and the Submeter version'; docs/17:189 'Every effective change'; raw.py:191 'an interval change, a provider falling back'. Adaptive switching is at docs/08:60, the overhead guard at docs/17:191 and the session interval override at docs/08:74. rollup.py:105,118 apply one epoch and one logical_cores per roll_up call; rollup.py:158-159: merge keeps latest.logical_cores and latest.epoch. The lead's merge_capacity.py re-ran identically: 'CPU 43200 s of 43200 core-seconds of capacity: 100% busy'; 'the merged hour keeps epoch 4 and logical_cores 16 ... = 75%'.
findings.impact: If adaptive switches count as epochs, which is how 'sampling intervals' and raw.py:191 read, a new epoch starts each time the machine goes quiet (idle_after 60 s), and R32's flag fires on almost every comparison. If they do not count, buckets mix 1 s and 5 s maxima with no record. A bucket that spans a hardware change shows a wrong percentage (75% against a true 100%), breaking docs/06:101.
findings.proposed_change: After the decision, write one definition in docs/06-storage.md:98 and copy it to docs/04:24, docs/08:5, docs/08:116, docs/17:130 and docs/17:189; align the raw.py:191 docstring. src/submeter/store/rollup.py: either make merge refuse mixed epochs, or give Bucket the minimum and maximum interval_s it contains and store capacity as core-seconds (the sum of covered_s x logical_cores), so a merged percentage stays right.
findings.cost: One paragraph and four one-line doc edits; about 10 lines in rollup.py and two Bucket fields.
findings.decision_question: Do changes the collector makes itself start an epoch: adaptive idle/active switching, the overhead guard lengthening intervals, a session's interval override? Options: (a) no; epochs track configured sampling settings, the rules file, provider status, hardware and version, and each bucket records the minimum and maximum interval it contains; (b) yes, every change in the interval actually used. And do alert, UI or verdict-setting edits start an epoch? Recommendation: (a), and no for alert, UI and verdict edits.
findings.verification: I re-ran merge_capacity.py and got identical output. Grepping docs/ for 'epoch' finds exactly the formulations above, and no sentence covers adaptive mode. R32 introduced epochs without addressing adaptive mode. I kept medium: a core-count change is rare (VM resize, CPU hot-plug), and the ambiguity in the definition corrupts no number until the epoch writer is built, but it decides whether R32's flags mean anything.

findings.title: daily_minimums applies one UTC offset to every reading, so local days are wrong across a daylight-saving change; the fix needs no tzdata
findings.evidence: growth.py:102-110: one 'utc_offset_s' is applied to every reading. docs/06:103 'Days and weeks are worked out in your time zone when you ask ... A day of 23 or 25 hours is compared per hour.' verify-6/v6_local_days.out.txt: 'offsets the OS gives across the window, in hours: [-5.0, -4.0]; fixed offset -5'; 'days whose fixed-offset minimum misses the nightly low: ['2026-11-01']'; 'Theil-Sen slope of daily minimums: fixed offset 9.63 MiB/day, per-reading offset 10.02 MiB/day (true 10.00)'; 'tzdata package installed: False'. Re-fetched https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html: astimezone() 'If called without arguments (or with tz=None) the system local time zone is assumed ... with the zone name and offset obtained from the OS.' The lead's local_days.py re-ran identically (Kolkata: '3 of 72 hourly buckets hold parts of two local days').
findings.impact: Across each daylight-saving change, the slow-growth check's daily minimums put an hour in the wrong day. In a 28-day synthetic leak the slope came out 4% low and one day lost its low. In half-hour zones, local days cut from hourly buckets are off by 30 minutes at each end. The effect on the trend job is small.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/analysis/growth.py daily_minimums: drop the fixed offset and take each reading's local day from datetime.fromtimestamp(t, UTC).astimezone(), which gets the offset from the OS with no new dependency. docs/06-storage.md:103: add 'in zones not a whole number of hours from UTC, local days built from hourly buckets are approximate by up to 30 minutes'. Do not add tzdata (AGENTS.md: no new dependency without approval) unless you want named zones other than the machine's own.
findings.cost: About 5 lines, a test, and one doc sentence.
findings.verification: I re-ran the lead's probe and got identical output. I also wrote v6_local_days.py to measure the effect on what the detector actually reads, not just bucket counts. I downgraded from medium to low because the slope moves by a few percent. I refuted the tzdata part: the per-reading OS offset needs no zone database package. That ran on Linux with tzdata absent; for Windows it rests on the Python docs' 'obtained from the OS' and was not run there. R35's intent stands; the baseline function cannot express it.

findings.title: choose_tier falls back to the minute tier without checking its retention, so it can answer from data that was already deleted
findings.evidence: query.py:40-50: the tier list depends only on the window's age against raw retention, and the point-budget fallback never checks the next tier's retention. config.py Retention has raw and minute durations with no ordering check. verify-6/v6_tiers.out.txt: '1. Retention(raw='60d', minute='30d') accepted'; '45 d back, 12 h -> minute step 60 s; covered: False'; '45 d back, 1 h -> minute step 60 s; covered: False'; '59 d back, 30 h -> minute step 60 s; covered: False'. docs/14:332 'Picks the finest tier whose retention still covers the start of the window.' docs/08:80 suggests raising retention.raw to 'Keep full detail longer'.
findings.impact: With raw retention set above minute retention, history windows 30 to 60 days back come back empty although the raw data exists. Default settings are not affected.
findings.proposed_change: src/submeter/store/query.py: drop any tier whose retention does not cover the window start; if only raw qualifies, return raw with a wider step. Alternatively, refuse retention.raw > retention.minute in config.py with the allowed range in the message. Add a test.
findings.verification: I re-ran interface_cases.py and got identical output. I wrote v6_tiers.py, which confirms the settings model accepts raw retention longer than minute retention and shows three uncovered answers. R33 sets the rule and docs/14 restates it; the code's fallback breaks it. Medium because it needs non-default settings, though docs/08 invites them.

findings.title: rollup.py merges hourly buckets from minute buckets; docs/05, R13 and docs/17 say hourly buckets are built from raw data
findings.evidence: rollup.py:9-10 'The same functions build minute buckets from raw samples and hourly buckets from minute buckets.' docs/05-data-flow.md:49 'Minute and hourly buckets are both built from raw data.'; docs/05:52 'Hourly buckets are built from raw data'; R13 (docs/16) 'Hourly rollups are computed from raw samples while those still exist'; docs/17:123 'Build hourly buckets from raw data while it still exists.' docs/14:316 'An hour merged from 60 minute buckets equals the hour built directly from samples' (tests/test_baseline.py:423-430).
findings.impact: R27's mergeable histograms made R13's requirement unnecessary, but the brief still ties hourly roll-ups to raw files, which may already be gone after server downtime (S2). A builder following docs/17:123 reads every raw file twice.
findings.proposed_change: docs/05-data-flow.md:49,52 and docs/17-build-prompt.md:123: 'Hourly buckets are merged from minute buckets.' Note in R13 that R27 superseded it.
findings.decision_question: The brief and the code disagree (AGENTS.md: say so and ask). Should hourly buckets be merged from minute buckets, as rollup.py does and R27 makes exact, or built from raw, as docs/05, docs/17 and R13 say? Recommendation: merge from minute buckets, and update the brief.
findings.verification: I re-read every cited line and the test. Both routes work with the baseline today (roll_up with width 3600 also builds from raw), so nothing fails and the impact is low. Neither route is more exact: merge inherits S10's latest-epoch problem, and a direct roll_up takes one logical_cores per call.
